program_note:
Lincoln Echoes is a “secular cantata,” written in honor of the 200th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln’s birth.  As this represents a contemporary look at an historical figure, the texts are drawn not only from the writings and speeches of Abraham Lincoln (spoken by the narrator), but also Franklin Delano Roosevelt (sung by the tenor soloist), and Barack Obama (sung by the baritone soloist).  In addition, the choir sings texts that are drawn from our founding documents—the Declaration of Independence and the United States Constitution—as well as a short excerpt by Martin Luther King, Jr.  Since some of the texts have other quotations within them (by Benjamin Franklin, George Washington, and—as primary authors of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, respectively—Thomas Jefferson and James Madison), the texts chosen for this cantata constitute a discussion of some of the most important issues of American governance from across the past 230 years.  The texts are printed below, and information on the sources is given on the last page of this score.

The music is in five movements.  The first two—Introduction: Fundamental Freedoms, featuring the choir and the narrator, and On Freedom and Democracy, featuring the three soloists, and the choir at the end—being primarily concerned with “pure ideas,” feature simpler harmonic language and are paired together.  The last three movements, On Freedom in the Face of Danger, On Economic Freedom, and On Freedom and Hope, featuring all three soloists, with the choir toward the end, all deal more with how we must deal with challenges American democracy has faced, and are thus also grouped together.  The last three movements run attacca into one another.

The music is approximately 36’ minutes in duration.

Lincoln Echoes was commissioned by the UCLA Center for the Liberal Arts and Free Institutions, for the gala concert celebrating their founding, and their Lincoln symposium.  It was written for Neal Stulberg, director of the UCLA Philharmonia, and Donald Neuen, director of the UCLA Chorale, and is dedicated to the memory of my father, Howard N. Lefkowitz, for whom these stirring words of freedom and individual and collective human rights were at the core of his legal thinking.

David S. Lefkowitz

Los Angeles, CA

13 October, 2009
